# FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision

Conference: ; ;

Wentao Zhang Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore ,
Yilei Zhao Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore ,
Guangyan Gan Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore ,
Shuo Sun Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
(Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China and Lin William Cong Note: Corresponding
author.  
Email (Wentao Zhang):
[zhangwent963@gmail.com](mailto:zhangwent963@gmail.com).
Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore

###### Abstract.

Public disclosure repositories such as SEC EDGAR support informed
investment through web access to corporate filings. Supporting their
review with language model agents requires discovering unstated
deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts,
and verifying that requested revisions satisfy evidence-backed
requirements. Existing financial question-answering evaluations provide
limited evidence of these interactive capabilities. We introduce
FilingLoop, an interactive benchmark and a self-evolving agent framework
for corporate disclosure review and revision. Grounded in historical
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission correspondence, FilingLoop
reconstructs 380 predominantly IPO review tasks from 96 companies under
distinct information constraints. An evaluator separate from the acting
agents scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible
requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Our
framework couples iterative review and revision within each case with
procedural learning across cases, converting requirement-level
evaluation feedback into role-specific guidance without updating model
weights. Updates affect only subsequent cases, allowing procedural
adaptation to be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the
evaluated stream, evolution increases requirement fulfillment from
24.28% to 27.96% and full comment resolution from 16.90% to 20.75%, with
a 5.8% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant. FilingLoop
connects the concerns an agent discovers with the company facts it
obtains and the revisions it commits, providing requirement-level
feedback for procedures used in later review tasks.

## 1. Introduction

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) provides public access
to corporate filings through its Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis,
and Retrieval (EDGAR) system, enabling investors to assess company
performance, risks, and accounting choices ([Healy and Palepu,
2001](#bib.bib1)). For companies preparing to go public, producing
reliable disclosures involves repeated exchanges between regulatory
reviewers and company counsel ([Johnston and Petacchi,
2017](#bib.bib2)).¹¹ 1
[https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/accessing-edgar-data](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/accessing-edgar-data)
Reviewers identify consequential gaps across filings and correspondence,
while counsel obtains facts and revises the relevant documents. As
illustrated in
Figure [1](#acmlabel1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision"),
a company may explain its 40% revenue growth simply as a result of
strong demand, without providing details about the factors driving that
growth. The information-access challenge is to discover omissions from
the evidence available at each review round and verify their resolution
in the appropriate document version.

percent revenue growth.](2610.37905v1/filingloop_overview.png)

Connecting issue discovery, evidence acquisition, and document revision
poses three challenges for agent evaluation. (1) Discovering unstated
issues. Financial question-answering and web-workflow benchmarks
evaluate predefined questions or tasks ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib6);
[Zhu et al., 2021](#bib.bib7); [Chen et al., 2022](#bib.bib8); [Islam et
al., 2023](#bib.bib9); [Krumdick et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Xie et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11); [Bigeard et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Drouin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15)), whereas reviewers must first determine which
disclosure gaps warrant scrutiny. (2) Acquiring missing facts. Agent
benchmarks evaluate tool use and interactive workflows, including web
tasks ([Liu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib13); [Mialon et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14); [Drouin et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)). Disclosure review
additionally requires targeted requests for company facts absent from
the public documents. (3) Verifying actual fulfillment. Interactive
benchmarks emphasize evaluation of final states ([Yao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16); [Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). In disclosure
review, each requirement must be checked against the relevant document.
A company may claim to have addressed a reviewer’s comment, but the
requirement remains unmet if the revised filing still lacks the
requested information.

The revenue example also shows why a persuasive response is
insufficient. Counsel must obtain a supported breakdown, place it in the
disclosure if requested, and check that the explanation remains
consistent with the rest of the filing. A response that merely promises
a revision leaves the disclosure unchanged. Conversely, a well-executed
amendment to one passage does not resolve other requests in the same
comment. Evaluating the entire sequence requires keeping track of what
was requested, what evidence became available, and what ultimately
changed in each document.

We evaluate _disclosure resolution_ in the final filing and response,
then use requirement-level feedback to improve review procedures on
later tasks. Reasoning-and-action agents, iterative refinement, and
learned workflows provide building blocks ([Yao et al.,
2022](#bib.bib19); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31)). Disclosure review requires tracing each concern from
source evidence to verified corrections across document versions.
Feedback on recurring investigation and verification failures can guide
reusable procedures ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22); [Yuksekgonul et
al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)), while
company-specific facts remain separate from transferable guidance.

To study these capabilities, we introduce FilingLoop, an interactive
benchmark and self-evolving agent framework grounded in historical SEC
initial public offering (IPO) review trajectories. Agents inspect full
filings while reference comments remain hidden. Reviewer and issuer
counsel operate under role-specific information constraints, with
evidence-bounded access to company facts. Independent evaluation checks
atomic requirements in final filings and responses and audits
unsupported claims and harmful actions. Evolving updates both roles’
guidance from completed cases after scores are locked; guidance is
frozen within batches and applies only to subsequent cases. Together,
the benchmark and framework offer three contributions:

- •
  Benchmark and framework. We reconstruct SEC review rounds, control
  access to historical records and company facts, and check each
  requested action in the final filing or response.
- •
  Procedural evolution for both roles. We distill requirement-level
  feedback into role-specific guidance, coupling iterative review and
  revision with procedural learning across cases while keeping model
  weights fixed throughout the ordered task stream.
- •
  Comprehensive evaluation. Across eight configurations on 380 tasks,
  FilingLoop–Evolving achieves the highest requirement and comment
  accuracies. Compared with Fixed, procedural evolution improves both
  discovery and conditional revision while reducing cost per fulfilled
  requirement.

## 2. Related Work

### 2.1. Financial Disclosure Analysis

Corporate disclosure reduces information gaps between firms and
investors. Healy and Palepu ([Healy and Palepu, 2001](#bib.bib1)) review
its relationship with information asymmetry and capital markets, while
Johnston and Petacchi ([Johnston and Petacchi, 2017](#bib.bib2)) examine
financial reporting oversight through SEC comment letters. This
literature motivates studying disclosure quality within the review
process. Financial language models provide complementary computational
capabilities: BloombergGPT ([Wu et al., 2023b](#bib.bib3)) incorporates
financial data into large-scale pretraining, and FinGPT ([Yang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib4)) develops an open framework for adapting language
models to downstream financial applications.

Financial benchmarks examine several capabilities needed to interpret
disclosures. FinQA ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib6)) and TAT-QA ([Zhu et
al., 2021](#bib.bib7)) test numerical reasoning over financial text and
tables; ConvFinQA ([Chen et al., 2022](#bib.bib8)) extends this setting
to conversational reasoning. FinanceBench ([Islam et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)) emphasizes evidence-supported answers from company
documents, whereas BizBench ([Krumdick et al., 2024](#bib.bib10))
examines quantitative reasoning and program synthesis. FinBen ([Xie et
al., 2024](#bib.bib11)) broadens evaluation to extraction, generation,
forecasting, and financial decision-making. ESGBenchmark ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37)) further evaluates environmental, social, and
governance (ESG) understanding and analysis based on corporate
sustainability reports. These benchmarks measure complementary aspects
of financial understanding, without making regulatory review and
document revision their central evaluation loop. Extracting a reported
number and assessing whether its explanation is adequate are different
objectives. Reviewers must identify omissions before receiving explicit
questions and obtain the facts needed to substantiate revisions.

Agentic financial research moves beyond isolated predictions.
FinRobot ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)) organizes specialized agents
and financial toolchains, while Finance Agent Benchmark ([Bigeard et
al., 2025](#bib.bib12)) evaluates expert-authored research questions
using search and SEC filings. Disclosure review adds a distinct
requirement: agents must discover consequential omissions, request
missing company facts, and substantiate corrections in the appropriate
documents. FilingLoop studies this process through a benchmark
reconstructed from historical SEC IPO review trajectories, with
evaluation of issue discovery and requirement fulfillment in final
filings and formal responses. Each reference concern states what must
change and the evidence supporting it, so we can check the final filing
and response against that request.

### 2.2. Interactive Agent Benchmarks

Interactive agents combine reasoning with actions that gather evidence
or change an environment. ReAct ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib19))
interleaves reasoning and tool use, while AgentBench ([Liu et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib13)) and GAIA ([Mialon et al., 2024](#bib.bib14))
evaluate agents across environments and realistic assistant tasks.
Effective evidence access remains a separate concern: Lost in the
Middle ([Liu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib18)) demonstrates that access to a
long context does not ensure reliable use of information throughout it.
Review therefore requires reliable evidence access across filings and
supporting documents.

Multi-agent frameworks structure collaboration through roles and
communication. AutoGen ([Wu et al., 2023a](#bib.bib26)) supports
configurable agent conversations, CAMEL ([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib28))
studies cooperation through role-playing, and MetaGPT ([Hong et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27)) organizes specialized roles around standard operating
procedures. Complementary benchmarks evaluate task completion in
operational settings. WorkArena ([Drouin et al., 2024](#bib.bib15))
evaluates browser-mediated enterprise tasks, and TheAgentCompany ([Xu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib30)) simulates digital work with tools and coworkers.
AppWorld ([Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)) evaluates resulting
application states and checks unintended changes. These settings assess
completed tasks and the consequences of agent actions, extending
evaluation beyond the quality of final replies.

Interaction itself can also determine success. $`\tau`$-bench ([Yao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib16)) combines user dialogue, domain policies, and
tools with final-state evaluation; $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench ([Barres et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)) extends coordination to a shared environment in which
both participants act. FilingLoop builds on these evaluation principles
through a regulatory reviewer and issuer counsel with distinct
responsibilities and information access. Their exchanges produce
revisions to a persistent filing, and an independent evaluator checks
whether each disclosure requirement is fulfilled in the relevant
deliverable, including checks for unsupported claims and harmful changes
to otherwise adequate disclosures.

### 2.3. Self-Evolving Agents

Feedback can improve both an agent’s current output and its behavior on
later tasks. Self-Refine ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib21)) iteratively
critiques and revises outputs, while Reflexion ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib20)) stores verbal feedback to guide subsequent trials.
For experience transfer, ExpeL ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22))
extracts insights from task trajectories, and Voyager ([Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib23)) accumulates executable skills during embodied
exploration. Agent Workflow Memory ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib31))
learns reusable routines for web navigation in offline and online
settings. These approaches retain experience as language, code, or
workflows without updating model weights. Applying experience transfer
to professional review requires role-specific procedures learned from
feedback on jointly produced documents.

Other work optimizes prompts and agent structures. Automatic Prompt
Engineer ([Zhou et al., 2022](#bib.bib32)) generates and selects
instructions, whereas OPRO ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)) conditions
new candidates on previous solutions and scores. ProTeGi ([Pryzant et
al., 2023](#bib.bib34)) combines textual critiques with search, and
TextGrad ([Yuksekgonul et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)) propagates textual
feedback through computation graphs. GEPA ([Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25)) uses trajectory reflection to evolve prompts and
combine complementary improvements. At the system level, Automated
Design of Agentic Systems ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)) searches over
code-defined agents, while AFlow ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)) uses
Monte Carlo tree search to construct agentic workflows. They edit
prompts or agent design and use varied feedback to select which of the
new versions to keep.

FilingLoop contributes a disclosure-review environment and an
evidence-linked feedback protocol for updating both professional roles
within a fixed workflow. Within-case review and revision are available
to both the evolving and fixed-policy agents; only the evolving group
carries learned guidance forward. Scores are locked before feedback is
released, skills are frozen within each batch, and updates apply only to
subsequent cases. The comparison evaluates a domain-specific application
of procedural reflection against a matched fixed-policy control, using
each task’s first-attempt score; it does not compare alternative
prompt-search algorithms.

## 3. FilingLoop

FilingLoop couples an interactive disclosure benchmark with a framework
for improving the procedures of agents acting as Reviewer and Filer.
Figure [3](#acmlabel3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3. FilingLoop ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
connects historical task construction, review and revision within a
case, and skill evolution across cases. This separation is essential:
both fixed and evolving agents can revise their work during an
interaction, but only the latter update their guidance for subsequent
tasks. We describe the benchmark and its evaluation criteria before
presenting the review and revision workflow and cross-case learning
procedure.

### 3.1. FilingLoop Benchmark

#### 3.1.1. Task Construction.

The benchmark reconstructs disclosure-review workflows from the SEC’s
public EDGAR archive, primarily covering IPO registration filings with a
small extension of annual reports from an existing issuer. Both domestic
and foreign companies are included. Filings, amendments, staff letters,
company responses, and exhibits retain their original identifiers and
dates to preserve provenance across document versions.

Records are grouped by company and review package, with administrative
correspondence distinguished from substantive responses. Within each
package, dates, references, comment numbers, and source spans establish
links between the reviewed filing, reviewer comments, company replies,
and subsequent revisions. For annual reports, the reporting period and
original accession must also be identified, as an SEC file number may
cover multiple reporting years. Recurring concerns are tracked as issue
threads across review rounds, while each occurrence retains its
supporting evidence and applicable requirements. This organization
allows the benchmark to trace how individual disclosure issues are
raised, addressed, and revisited across successive review rounds.

Each task reconstructs one historical review round using a fixed local
snapshot of permitted EDGAR records. Agents see the reviewed filing and
earlier history; current historical comments, replies, and subsequent
amendments remain hidden. Document visibility follows the reconstructed
review history, which may differ from the dates on which correspondence
became public. The hidden reference decomposes compound comments into
atomic requirements, each linked to a disposition, target deliverable,
supporting evidence, applicable comment IDs, and any required company
facts. Construction combines model-assisted annotation, independent
checking, reconciliation, and source validation. The project team
verified the original collection. Annual-report records underwent
additional annotation and audit passes with exact source checks. Model
agreement is not treated as measured label accuracy.

Task eligibility is determined before agent execution. A scored comment
must be identifiable from the permitted records and contain at least one
applicable requirement supported by the available evidence. Requirements
that depend on company facts are retained only when those facts can be
attributed to evidence from the current round. Ambiguous source links
and unsupported requirements are preserved in the audit trail rather
than resolved through inference. Registration effectiveness is not
considered evidence that a filing has no remaining deficiencies, and
therefore does not serve as a basis for constructing negative tasks.
Figure [2](#acmlabel2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
summarizes the evaluable collection. Filing lengths are measured by
whitespace-separated word counts in the primary filing for each task,
excluding documents provided as prior-round history.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
details reconstruction, annotation, and eligibility checks.

Eligibility and the unit of annotation. The discovery pool contained 300
company candidates. Reconstruction yielded 412 review rounds, of which
380 are eligible; the other 32 remain in exclusion records. A further 93
terminal diagnostics are excluded because effectiveness or closure does
not establish the absence of disclosure deficiencies. Fact-evidence
checks remove 318 requirement occurrences lacking the necessary
current-round support. The retained tasks therefore measure resolution
where the requested action and its evidentiary basis can be
reconstructed, rather than treating every archived exchange as scorable.

A requirement specifies an action and its expected deliverable, rather
than a string that must be copied from the historical response. Filing
changes, explanations to staff, supporting material, and commitments are
checked in their respective artifacts. A comment containing several such
requests is decomposed so that a supported explanation does not earn
credit for an unmade amendment. Requirements are attached to the rounds
in which they apply: a later follow-up does not retroactively add an
obligation to an earlier task. Repeated requests remain separate
occurrences when they recur in later rounds.
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3. Atomic Requirements and Evidence Verification ‣ Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
details annotation and reconciliation, and
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4. Scoring Eligibility and Corpus Coverage ‣ Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")

coverage.

#### 3.1.2. Task Characteristics.

The benchmark contains 380 review tasks from 96 companies and 98 review
packages, with 3,012 scorable comments and 6,099 applicable requirement
occurrences. These levels are distinct: one task can contain many
comments, and a recurring issue can contribute requirements in more than
one round. The 378 registration tasks span 97 packages. Another 2 tasks
come from one issuer’s annual-report review in 2026. This deliberately
small extension adds no companies and does not establish broad
annual-report coverage.
Figure [2](#acmlabel2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
reports distributions recomputed using the same eligibility rules as the
evaluation harness. All eligible tasks form a single evaluation stream,
with no separate training or validation split. The online protocol below
permits learning only from already scored tasks.

These statistics identify three demands on the agents. First, agents
must discover multiple issues within a filing: the median task contains
4 scorable comments, with a 90th percentile of 21. Second, 62.7% of
comments contain multiple requirements, so addressing one request need
not resolve the whole comment. Third, 50.5% of requirements are marked
as needing company facts. Disclosure changes account for 76.5% of
requirements; the remainder call for explanations to staff, supporting
material, or commitments. These are disposition types, not financial
topic labels. They motivate evaluation of discovery, evidence
acquisition, and verification in the required document.
Section [4](#S4 "4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
examines how effectively agents meet these demands in the evaluated task
stream.

#### 3.1.3. Outcome Evaluation.

An evaluator separate from the acting Reviewer assesses frozen artifacts
using one grading model in three stages. (1) Matching aligns generated
comments with historical concerns by substance and requested action; a
grounded additional concern is not automatically an error.
(2) Fulfillment checks all requirements of matched scorable comments in
one case-level request, sharing the complete final filing across
judgments. Each requirement receives a binary verdict, an artifact
identifier, a supporting quotation when available, and a reason.
Disclosure changes require evidence in the final filing; a promise in a
reply does not suffice. (3) Audit jointly checks extracted company
assertions and all final-document changes against permitted source
evidence and released facts. Missing support alone is distinguished from
a contradiction.

Applicable evaluation stages return schema-constrained JSON. The
controller checks identifier coverage and quotation provenance before
computing scores. Invalid outputs are retried, and persistent failures
remain incomplete assessments. Case-level evaluation shares the final
filing across comments without resubmitting it. These checks establish
structure and source provenance; semantic validity still depends on
interpreting the evidence and requested disclosure changes. Human–grader
agreement and cross-grader sensitivity are not quantified.

Each assessment records discovery, requirement fulfillment, full comment
resolution, and harm. Discovery credits a reference concern when it
matches a generated comment. End-to-end fulfillment requires both
discovery of the concern and verification of the requested action in its
final deliverable. A comment is fully resolved only when all its
requirements pass. Undiscovered concerns and their requirements remain
in the respective denominators, so missed issues cannot inflate
accuracy.

Harm records unfounded additional concerns, comments with contradicted
company assertions, and tasks containing harmful filing changes. These
counts supplement accuracy without being subtracted from it.
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
describes aggregate accuracies, role diagnostics, completion, and
resources;
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
gives their formal definitions and reporting scopes.

### 3.2. Self-Evolving Agents

#### 3.2.1. Review and Revision.

The two roles use a common language model with distinct instructions,
outputs, and information access. The Reviewer inspects permitted
documents and raises grounded concerns with source references. The Filer
responds to these concerns, requests missing company information when
needed, and submits concrete revisions. Both roles use document-reading
and shell tools in isolated workspaces containing the allowed record and
navigation aids. Hidden references are held by the environment, not
copied into actor workspaces. Persistent documents and structured state
carry the interaction across turns rather than relying on an
unrestricted shared conversation history.

Revisions are submitted as source replacements linked to comment IDs.
The controller accepts a replacement only when its target can be located
uniquely, allowing whitespace normalization but rejecting ambiguous
matches. Accepted changes are committed to the authoritative draft. If a
response also requests facts, completed edits are preserved while the
Filer finalizes the pending work after receiving an answer. The fact
service releases only evidence-supported information linked to the
relevant current-round comments. Released facts enter the Filer’s
private history, while the Reviewer sees the resulting formal responses
and disclosures. An empty service answer indicates limited evidence
coverage, not that the real company possesses no information.

The Reviewer then reassesses the revised filing and responses.
Unresolved comments and newly raised concerns can initiate another
exchange, with prior responses and committed revisions preserved.
Detailed rereview rationales are logged for audit rather than forwarded
to the next Filer turn. Interaction ends when no active work remains or
the exchange budget is exhausted. This stopping decision controls
execution only: final scoring retains all eligible requirements,
including concerns the Reviewer did not raise or close. The fixed-policy
baseline shares this workflow, providing a matched control for the joint
skill updates applied to subsequent cases under identical base prompts.

#### 3.2.2. Information and Artifact Control.

Both roles can inspect the permitted record and current draft, but their
private conversations remain separate. Fact requests and released
answers enter the Filer’s history. The Reviewer can use that information
only when the Filer includes it in a formal response or the revised
disclosure. The service withholds reference identifiers and original
historical replies, so acquiring facts does not reveal the hidden
comment letter. Its answers retain their status as company statements
supported by the archived evidence; the fact service does not
independently certify the company’s underlying analyses or commitments.

The authoritative draft also remains separate from workspace files.
Ordered edit transactions identify the source text, replacement, and
motivating comment IDs; the host records whether each operation was
committed. Supporting-document changes additionally identify the
authorized artifact and its base hash. This distinction matters when an
agent reports a change that its edit failed to apply. After a fact
request, finalization receives the current draft and edit outcomes,
retains committed work, and addresses pending responses and rejected
edits. It cannot initiate another fact request within that phase.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2. Tools, Submissions, and Committed Artifacts ‣ Appendix B Task Environment and Interaction Protocol ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
gives the submission contracts, and
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3. Bounded Company-Fact Acquisition ‣ Appendix B Task Environment and Interaction Protocol ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
describes fact release and finalization.

#### 3.2.3. Online Skill Evolution.

We evaluate procedural adaptation through an ordered task stream,
pooling all eligible cases. A seeded company order and round-robin
scheduling preserve chronological order within each company; a batch
contains at most one task per company. Both experimental arms receive
the same ordered batches, base prompts, model, tools, and execution
budgets, starting with empty learned skills. Task concurrency controls
scheduling within a batch independently of the batch size. Skills remain
frozen until every task in both arms has completed execution and
scoring. Thus, completion order cannot change the guidance available to
other tasks running concurrently in that batch.

After first-attempt results are locked, a skill editor receives the
evolving arm’s completed-batch feedback: discovery outcomes, applicable
requirements, fulfillment decisions, evidence quotations, and reasons.
It proposes reusable procedural guidance separately for the Reviewer and
Filer, or explicitly retains the current guidance. Let $`s_{b}^{r}`$
denote the frozen skill used by role $`r`$ (Reviewer or Filer) in batch
$`b`$, and $`\mathcal{F}_{b}`$ the evolving arm’s locked batch feedback.
The update is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1) |     |

````math
s_{b+1}^{r}=\operatorname{ValidateOrKeep}\bigl(\operatorname{Edit}(s_{b}^{r},\mathcal{F}_{b}),s_{b}^{r}\bigr).
``` |  |

Validation checks structure, role identity, company identifiers, and
direct copying of reference text. Invalid proposals can be revised using
validation feedback; if no valid update is produced, the incumbent skill
is retained. Guidance length is advisory; accepted updates are not
truncated. Validation enforces content and formatting constraints
without selecting updates by held-out performance.

Only later, unattempted tasks use the new guidance. Model weights and
base instructions remain fixed, completed cases retain their original
scores, and skill updates stop after the penultimate batch. We record
skill versions, update decisions, task outcomes, elapsed time, and model
usage, including editing costs. This is online adaptation with
historical scoring feedback, not evaluation on an independent held-out
test set. Earlier rounds of a company may inform later rounds;
unseen-company generalization requires a separate evaluation protocol.

What transfers between tasks. Each skill is a Markdown document with
role metadata and procedural instructions. Reviewer guidance can specify
how to inspect an explanation for missing evidence; Filer guidance can
specify how to verify a committed change against every request in a
compound comment. These are procedures that the representation can
express, rather than new facts about the next issuer. Fixed role
instructions take precedence, and any assertion about the current issuer
still requires support from its permitted records or company facts that
the service releases for that issuer’s current review round.

The editor can return no_change or a complete replacement skill. It
receives validation errors for invalid proposals and has at most three
attempts per role. Known company identifiers, private source paths, and
sufficiently long exact reference copies are rejected. These textual
checks constrain what is retained without establishing that every
paraphrased case detail has been removed. Incompletely assessed batches
produce no update. Policy hashes bind each subsequent task to the
guidance frozen before it starts, allowing the recorded outcome to be
related to the procedure actually available during execution.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Procedural Evolution ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
provides the skill format, validation rules, and update schedule.

## 4. Empirical Studies

We evaluate discovery, fulfillment, resource use, and harmful revisions
under fixed and evolving policies. Our study addresses four research
questions:

- •
  RQ1: How effectively do FilingLoop and existing agents discover and
  resolve disclosure deficiencies across backbones?
- •
  RQ2: How does cross-task procedural evolution affect end-to-end
  resolution and role-level performance?
- •
  RQ3: What are the trade-offs between resolution quality, token usage,
  monetary cost, and execution time?
- •
  RQ4: How often do filing revisions introduce harm, and how completely
  are they audited?

### 4.1. Experimental Setup

Data and task stream. The evaluation uses all 380 eligible review tasks
from 96 companies in the benchmark described in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1. FilingLoop Benchmark ‣ 3. FilingLoop ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").
These comprise 378 registration-review tasks and 2 annual-report tasks,
pooled without a training or validation split. All configurations
receive the same seeded company order, chronological rounds within each
company, and permitted records. Current historical comments, subsequent
replies, and amendments remain hidden from the acting agents throughout
each task.

Online protocol. Each task is attempted once per stream. Both FilingLoop
variants start with empty learned skills and identical base
instructions. The main comparison uses order seed 0 and batches of at
most 16 tasks, with no repeated company within a batch. Skills remain
frozen until both variants finish scoring the batch. The evolving
variant then updates its guidance using its own locked feedback,
exclusively for subsequent tasks. Scores are never replaced by replay
results; earlier company rounds may nevertheless inform later rounds
under this online adaptation protocol. The reported differences describe
this seeded stream and are limited to the evaluated task sample and
order.

Execution and assessment. The reference configuration permits up to
three review–revision exchanges and 100 agent steps per role invocation,
including follow-up phases. A step is one model response and its
resulting tool calls. We run up to 16 tasks concurrently and record
resource usage separately for each role invocation. A single gpt-6.1-sol
grader assesses frozen artifacts through the matching, fulfillment, and
audit stages in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1. FilingLoop Benchmark ‣ 3. FilingLoop ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").
The same model performs fact matching and skill editing, with
grading-policy identifiers retained for each assessment. The evaluator
was manually reviewed; all configurations use the same grading model,
prompts, and artifact checks. Acting roles receive no current-task
grading feedback. Manifests record model identifiers, inference
settings, software versions, data fingerprints, and policy versions. We
use high as the default LLM reasoning effort; inference options are
retained in the execution manifests. Because step definitions differ
across frameworks, we report measured token usage, cost, and execution
time alongside nominal step budgets.
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Experimental Configuration and Reproducibility ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
gives construction, information boundaries, and reproduction details.

### 4.2. Evaluation Metrics

Requirement and comment resolution. For task $`t`$, let
$`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$ be the scorable reference comments and
$`\mathcal{U}_{ti}`$ the applicable requirements of comment $`i`$. Let
$`d_{ti}\in\{0,1\}`$ indicate discovery of that comment and
$`b_{tij}\in\{0,1\}`$ indicate fulfillment of requirement $`j`$ in its
requested deliverable. Over the evaluated task set $`\mathcal{T}`$,
system accuracies are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| (2) |  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}_{\rm req}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U}_{ti}}d_{ti}b_{tij}}{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}|\mathcal{U}_{ti}|},`$ |  |
| (3) |  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}_{\rm comment}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}d_{ti}\prod_{j\in\mathcal{U}_{ti}}b_{tij}}{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\mathcal{C}_{t}|}.`$ |  |

All accuracies are reported as percentages. Requirement Accuracy gives
equal weight to annotated requirement occurrences, while Comment
Accuracy gives equal weight to comments and requires every constituent
obligation to pass. The denominators are fixed before execution. Missing
a concern therefore earns no system credit without removing the concern
or its requirements. Requirements can share evidence or prerequisites;
their count represents annotated obligations rather than independent
causes of failure.

Task and company resolution. Task Accuracy is the fraction of tasks for
which assessment is complete and every applicable requirement passes.
Company Accuracy requires the same condition across all review rounds of
an issuer. These stricter measures withhold a pass when even one
obligation remains unmet. Task completion instead measures whether
execution and assessment finish, independently of resolution quality.
Failed or unassessed tasks receive no system credit, and their known
reference targets remain in the system denominators.

Reviewer and Filer diagnostics. Reviewer scores measure discovery over
the full reference inventory. Requirement-level discovery credit
inherits the parent-comment match; it does not imply that the Reviewer
separately articulated every atomic requirement. Post-hoc Filer scores
compare the two variants on Fixed’s assigned reference-comment IDs:
2,162 requirements from 983 comments, covering 283 tasks and 95
companies. Both Filer numerators retain only fulfillment linked to those
IDs. Extra Evolving discoveries contribute to system scores, while tasks
and companies with no assigned targets are excluded from the conditional
Filer accuracies.

This common pool fixes the scope of the diagnostic, rather than the
comments shown to the agents. Each Filer still receives its own
Reviewer’s requests and retains the interaction that produced its final
artifacts. Consequently, the paired Filer scores describe fulfillment
under the joint policies; they do not isolate the effect of updating
Filer alone. Reviewer and Filer scores describe different stages and are
not additive contributions to system accuracy.

Harm and audit coverage. The evaluator separately checks unfounded
additional concerns, contradicted company assertions, and harmful filing
changes. A harmful revision introduces unsupported claims or
contradictions, or damages supported disclosure; leaving an original
request unresolved is not itself harm. The task-level harm rate counts
audited tasks containing at least one such change, whereas edit-audit
coverage counts audited tasks among all scheduled tasks. Unaudited tasks
are excluded from the harm-rate denominator rather than treated as
harm-free. These measures supplement fulfillment without being
subtracted from the accuracy scores.

Resources and efficiency. We report input/output tokens, API cost,
cumulative Agent hours, and mean minutes per scheduled task. Input
includes cache reads and writes; Output includes reasoning tokens. Cost
applies the saved price schedule to recorded usage for role execution
and shared services, including assessment, fact matching, and skill
editing. It is a usage-based total rather than a reconciled invoice
amount. Shared services remain in the system total, so the displayed
role costs need not account for all expenditure needed to produce and
assess the final artifacts.

Agent hours sum recorded role-invocation durations, including model
calls, tools, and compaction, while excluding independent assessment and
gaps between stopping and restarting. Concurrent tasks each contribute
their own duration. Mean minutes per task uses all 380 scheduled tasks;
missing duration segments are not imputed. Cost per fulfilled
requirement divides total system cost by the fulfilled requirement
count, and throughput uses either that cost or cumulative Agent time.
These ratios describe resource use per observed outcome, rather than
elapsed wall-clock speed.
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
gives the complete role-scoped formulas, failure handling, and
accounting conventions.

### 4.3. Baselines

We compare three external agent frameworks and two FilingLoop variants.
Codex, paired with gpt-6.1-sol, supports non-interactive execution and
structured event logging.²² 2
[https://developers.openai.com/codex/noninteractive](https://developers.openai.com/codex/noninteractive)
Claude Code, paired with claude-opus-5.5, provides file-reading,
editing, and shell tools within its agent loop.³³ 3
[https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless)
mini-SWE-agent provides a lightweight shell-based scaffold and is paired
with gpt-6.1-sol, claude-opus-5.5, gemini-4-argon, and
deepseek-v4.1-flash.⁴⁴ 4
[https://mini-swe-agent.com/latest/](https://mini-swe-agent.com/latest/)
Both FilingLoop variants use gpt-6.1-sol: FilingLoop–Fixed retains the
review–revision workflow without skill updates, while
FilingLoop–Evolving also learns role-specific guidance from locked
historical feedback. These pairings yield eight comparison
configurations, with the same backbone assigned to both roles within
each configuration. External adapters preserve separate role sessions,
equal access to permitted records and scoped facts, and the common
artifact-submission contract, while retaining each framework’s native
execution loop. Fixed configurations carry no learned guidance between
tasks. The gpt-6.1-sol configurations control model choice when
comparing frameworks, while the four mini-SWE-agent configurations
compare backbones within a common scaffold. The FilingLoop pair compares
fixed guidance with cross-task procedural evolution.

### 4.4. Main Results (RQ1)

End-to-end resolution.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
compares eight configurations across four levels of disclosure
resolution. FilingLoop–Evolving achieves the highest Requirement and
Comment Accuracies, 27.96% and 20.75%, fulfilling 1,705 requirements and
fully resolving 625 comments. Relative to the strongest external
baseline, mini-SWE-agent with claude-opus-5.5, these are gains of 4.22
and 4.38 percentage points (pp), respectively.
Figure [4](#acmlabel4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4. Main Results (RQ1) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")(a)
compares fulfillment of individual requirements with resolution of
entire comments, which requires all constituent checks to pass.

Framework and backbone comparisons. With the same gpt-6.1-sol backbone,
FilingLoop–Fixed reaches 24.28% Requirement Accuracy, exceeding Codex by
2.15 pp and mini-SWE-agent by 2.29 pp. The fixed review–revision
workflow thus already resolves more reference requirements in the
reported comparison, before procedural updates. Within mini-SWE-agent,
changing the backbone yields Requirement Accuracy from 19.56% (DeepSeek)
to 23.74% (Opus), showing that performance depends on both the model and
its execution framework under the shared task and scoring protocol.

Four colored panels in one horizontal row compare the eight
configurations in the main table. Evolving achieves the highest
requirement and comment accuracies, 27.96 and 20.75 percent. Relative to
Fixed it fulfills 224 more requirements and fully resolves 116 more
comments. The cost plot places Evolving above Fixed in accuracy with a
modest increase in cost. Relative gains of 15.1 percent in fulfilled
requirements and 22.8 percent in resolved comments accompany increases
of 5.8 percent in cost and 3.1 percent in recorded Agent time. Cost per
fulfilled requirement falls by 8.1 percent.

Accuracy; (b) Fixed–Evolving comparison; (c) cost versus Requirement

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").Four
colored panels in one horizontal row compare the eight configurations in

Relative gains of 15.1 percent in fulfilled requirements and 22.8

and 3.1 percent in recorded Agent time. Cost per fulfilled requirement

Execution completion versus substantive success. All configurations
complete at least 99.21% of scheduled tasks, yet none exceeds 5.26% Task
Accuracy. The highest Task Accuracy is achieved by mini-SWE-agent/Opus
with 20 fully successful tasks, compared with 19 for Evolving. Evolving
leads at company level, but only 2 of 96 companies pass all requirements
across their review rounds; every external configuration has zero
company-level passes. These stricter metrics distinguish partial
improvement from complete resolution of all obligations in a review
round or company trajectory.
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Case Studies and Failure Analysis ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
provides artifact-linked success and compound-request failure cases with
the relevant filing passages and responses.

Findings (RQ1). (1) Fixed’s advantage is present before evolution. Fixed
exceeds the other gpt-6.1-sol configurations in Requirement Accuracy
before evolution. This compares complete frameworks without isolating
role prompts, tools, or document management. (2) The task-level ranking
differs from the pooled scores. Evolving leads in Requirement Accuracy
but not Task Accuracy. Every requested action must pass in its target
filing or formal response before a concern is fully resolved.
(3) Unresolved obligations persist across issuer rounds. Outstanding
obligations span review rounds; recurring concerns and related
requirements are not independent observations.

Gains across evaluation levels.
Figure [5](#acmlabel5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.5. Effect of Procedural Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")(a)
compares Fixed and Evolving across four system metrics under the online
protocol, where updates affect only subsequent tasks. Requirement
Accuracy rises from 24.28% to 27.96% (+3.68 pp), and Comment Accuracy
from 16.90% to 20.75% (+3.85 pp). This corresponds to 224 additional
fulfilled requirements and 116 additional fully resolved comments over
the same reference inventory. Task Accuracy increases from 3.95% to
5.00%, while Company Accuracy increases from 1.04% to 2.08%. These are
observed gains in this stream; company-level success changes from one
issuer to two.

Discovery and conditional revision.
Figure [5](#acmlabel5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.5. Effect of Procedural Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")(b)
separates discovery from conditional revision. Reviewer Requirement and
Comment Accuracies improve by 1.41 and 1.29 pp, respectively. On the
shared Fixed target pool, Filer Requirement Accuracy increases by 10.36
pp to 78.86%, and Comment Accuracy increases by 11.80 pp to 63.58%. The
pool controls scoring scope; each Filer still responds to its own
Reviewer. These are conditional diagnostics of the joint policy.

Remaining coverage gap. Even with evolution, Reviewer covers only 36.86%
of reference requirements and 33.93% of reference comments. Filer’s
higher conditional accuracy applies only to assigned concerns; it cannot
compensate for undiscovered deficiencies. Evolution improves resolution
across the task stream, with further gains constrained by issue
discovery.

Accounting for the residual errors. Under Evolving, 3,851 requirements
remain undiscovered and 543 are discovered but unfulfilled. The
undiscovered group accounts for 87.6% of all remaining unfulfilled
requirements. This decomposition uses each variant’s own discovery set;
it is distinct from the shared Fixed pool used for paired Filer
accuracy. Relative to Fixed, discovery rises by 86 requirements while
the discovered but unfulfilled count falls by 138, giving the net gain
of $`86+138=224`$. The corresponding comment-level identity is
$`39+77=116`$. These aggregate identities locate the remaining workload
without identifying item-level transitions or assigning causal effects
to either role.
Appendix [G.2](#A7.SS2 "G.2. Discovery and Fulfillment Bottlenecks ‣ Appendix G Extended Results and Analyses ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
gives the complete residual accounting.

Findings (RQ2). (1) Joint updates improve the recorded scores. Evolving
increases all four system accuracies with fixed model weights and
first-pass scoring. Attributing gains requires role-specific update
ablations.
Appendix [H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3. Procedural Transfer Across Cases ‣ Appendix H Case Studies and Failure Analysis ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
traces a learned verification procedure into a later filing. (2) Role
gains use different target sets. Reviewer covers all references; Filer
conditions on Fixed’s targets. Their percentage-point changes are not
additive contributions to system gain. (3) Undiscovered concerns cap
system accuracy. Even perfect revision of Evolving’s discovered set caps
system Requirement Accuracy at 36.86%. Expanding discovery is necessary
to resolve additional reference obligations.

requirements; hours denote recorded Agent time. SWE = mini-SWE-agent;
backbones follow
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

Incremental cost of evolution. Evolving costs \$2,519.23 across 380
tasks, compared with \$2,380.15 for Fixed, an increase of 5.8%. Recorded
Agent time increases by 3.1%, from 455.04 to 469.36 hours, or 2.26
additional minutes per task. Input and output tokens increase by 5.5%
and 6.5%, respectively. In comparison, the numbers of fulfilled
requirements and fully resolved comments grow by 15.1% and 22.8%
(Figure [4](#acmlabel4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4. Main Results (RQ1) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")(d)).
Token and cost totals include skill editing and subsequent execution
under the updated policies; Agent time measures recorded role
invocations.

Resolution per unit of expenditure. The larger outcome gains reduce cost
per fulfilled requirement from \$1.61 to \$1.48, an improvement of 8.1%.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.6. Resource Efficiency (RQ3) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
reports normalized cost and throughput for all configurations. Evolving
resolves more requirements per dollar and per recorded Agent hour than
Fixed, although several external configurations have higher throughput
at lower overall accuracy. In particular, mini-SWE-agent/DeepSeek offers
the highest requirement throughput per dollar and hour, but the lowest
Requirement Accuracy, 19.56%. Efficiency and coverage must therefore be
considered jointly when choosing an operating point.

Cross-framework trade-offs.
Figure [4](#acmlabel4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4. Main Results (RQ1) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")(c)
shows that Evolving achieves higher accuracy while costing 28.0% less
than Codex and 32.2% less than Claude Code. Mini-SWE-agent uses less
recorded Agent time than either FilingLoop variant. Throughput uses
cumulative recorded invocation time, excluding pauses and independent
assessment; missing segments are not imputed. These rates measure
recorded work rather than wall-clock speed
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")).

Where the additional cost occurs. The \$139.08 increase comprises
\$41.20 in Reviewer-attributed usage, \$53.30 in Filer-attributed usage,
and \$44.58 in shared services. It therefore includes both producing
guidance and executing and assessing the resulting behavior. The entire
difference should not be interpreted as the price of the skill editor
alone. Dividing the extra cost by the net requirement gain gives \$0.62
per additional fulfilled requirement on this stream; this descriptive
ratio does not estimate the cost of resolving any particular remaining
request.
Appendix [G.4](#A7.SS4 "G.4. Role and Shared-Service Resources ‣ Appendix G Extended Results and Analyses ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
separates role usage from shared-service resources.

Findings (RQ3). (1) Evolution lowers cost per fulfilled requirement.
Evolving spends more per task, but its cost per fulfilled requirement
falls by 8.1%. These usage-based benchmark costs depend on the service
mix. (2) More spending need not resolve more requirements. Codex and
Claude Code incur higher cost and Agent time while fulfilling fewer
requirements. Additional calls should target unresolved requests and
verify committed amendments. (3) Selective escalation requires separate
evaluation. Mini-SWE-agent’s higher throughput suggests a low-cost first
pass with targeted escalation; we do not test a cascade here.

### 4.7. Harmful Revisions (RQ4)

We measure harmful revisions at the task level: a task is flagged if at
least one filing change is judged harmful against permitted evidence and
released company facts. Among tasks with completed edit audits, Fixed
has a harmful-revision rate of 5.8%, compared with 4.5% for Evolving.
Higher fulfillment under evolution thus coincides with a 1.3 pp lower
observed harm rate. Each affected task contributes one flag regardless
of its edit count, so this comparison describes harm prevalence across
tasks without quantifying the severity of individual changes. Edit-audit
coverage is 99.74% and 100% of scheduled tasks, respectively
(Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2. Task Completion and Harm Audits ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision"));
unaudited tasks are excluded from the harm-rate denominator. Full
coverage provides an audit outcome for every scheduled task, including
those with harmful edits. Both variants still produce harmful changes,
so the audit complements fulfillment scores by checking whether
requested revisions introduce new errors into the filing.

A task can fulfill a reference request and still be flagged for an
unsupported change elsewhere. It can also leave a request unresolved
without introducing a harmful edit. The two measures therefore answer
different questions about the same final filing. Full audit coverage
means that every scheduled task received an edit-audit outcome; it does
not mean that every interaction met the joint completion criterion, nor
that every change was harmless. Thus Evolving’s 100% edit-audit coverage
is consistent with its 99.74% task completion in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

These rates describe the joint evolving policy under a common audit
protocol. Establishing whether either role’s updated guidance prevents
specific errors, or reduces their severity, would require edit-level
comparisons and role-specific update ablations.

## 5. Conclusion

We introduced FilingLoop, an interactive benchmark and self-evolving
agent framework grounded in archived SEC EDGAR disclosure reviews. Its
evaluation connects issue discovery and evidence acquisition to verified
fulfillment in final filings and responses. Across 380 tasks from 96
companies in the evaluated stream, the joint evolving policy improves
requirement fulfillment and full comment resolution, while reducing cost
per fulfilled requirement by 8.1%, without changing model weights or
retrying scored tasks. The role-level results reveal a key bottleneck:
improved revision cannot compensate for undiscovered deficiencies.
Further progress therefore calls for agents that actively uncover
omissions, retain unresolved obligations across review rounds, and
verify every requested change in its intended deliverable. FilingLoop
records how agents investigate omissions, obtain company facts, and
revise the relevant documents, giving the skill editor a record of which
requested actions were fulfilled and which remain unresolved after the
final response.

Contents of Appendix

## Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction

Construction separates historical source documents, cross-round issue
threads, and task-specific requirements
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1. FilingLoop Benchmark ‣ 3. FilingLoop ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")).
Source evidence fixes eligibility before agents inspect documents, raise
comments, or revise disclosures.

### A.1. Source Corpus and Document Provenance

The collection began with 300 company candidates selected by
year-stratified sampling of registration activity in EDGAR quarterly
indexes. This discovery pool includes records that do not yield eligible
benchmark tasks. The evaluated corpus contains 96 companies and 98
review packages: 97 registration-review packages and 1 annual-report
package. Eligible review events span May 2016 to March 2026. These dates
refer to the historical reviews, rather than the time at which records
were collected or became publicly accessible. EDGAR correspondence is
released after the associated review process, so its public availability
date can differ from the date of the underlying exchange.⁵⁵ 5 SEC
guidance on correspondence and its release:
[https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/how-search-edgar-correspondence](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/how-search-edgar-correspondence).

Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A.1. Source Corpus and Document Provenance ‣ Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
summarizes source groups and data types. Source identities, hashes, and
evidence spans link records to their original submissions. Document
dates order the review history; filing dates are preserved separately.
Only permitted earlier records enter agent workspaces; current
correspondence and later amendments remain hidden reference evidence.
The format strip distinguishes archived document members from processed
representations: normalized text and structured records support
reconstruction and source tracing, while original submission files
retain their source identity.

### A.2. Package, Round, and Issue Reconstruction

A registration-review package groups filing versions and correspondence
using file numbers, form families, dates, and explicit letter
references. Issuer correspondence is classified to distinguish
substantive responses from acceleration and withdrawal requests.
Retained links record their supporting basis, while ambiguous
relationships remain in audit records.

Each substantive staff letter defines a review round. The reconstruction
binds it to the reviewed filing, aligns numbered comments with issuer
responses, and identifies the associated revision when one exists.
Alignment uses comment numbers, repeated comment text, and references to
the staff letter; supplemental replies can provide evidence for
individual comments. Revision evidence comprises uniquely anchored text
replacements or relevant differences between the bound versions.
Page-level differences can include unrelated financial or offering
updates, so they require interpretation against the requested action.
Comment and response spans retain source locations, including requests
and answers continued across page boundaries.

References to earlier comments connect recurring concerns into issue
threads. Each occurrence nevertheless remains attached to its own round
and reviewed version. A task begins before that round’s review: agents
receive the filing and permitted history, while the current letter,
replies, and subsequent revisions remain hidden. This separation
preserves the Reviewer’s need to discover issues independently.

### A.3. Atomic Requirements and Evidence Verification

Annotations decompose an issue thread into independently checkable
requirements supported by the historical response and revision evidence.
Each requirement records its requested action, disposition type,
supporting quotation, applicable comment identifiers, and any required
company facts. The four disposition types and their expected
deliverables are summarized in
Table [3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ A.3. Atomic Requirements and Evidence Verification ‣ Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").
A request to amend a disclosure is distinct from a request to explain it
to staff, supply supporting material, or make a future commitment.
Historical responses establish an evidence-supported resolution, while
requirements describe the action to be satisfied rather than requiring
agents to reproduce the historical wording or copy the company’s exact
response.

The registration-review annotations use an initial gpt-6-astra
annotation and an independent claude-opus-5.5 audit. The auditor reviews
the proposed requirements and facts while independently determining
handling and answerability without seeing the annotator’s decisions for
those fields. Disagreements undergo reconciliation and a further audit;
quotation checks verify support in the supplied sources. The
annual-report extension uses separate annotation and audit calls to
gpt-6.1-sol, followed by reconciliation, comment mapping, and source
verification. The project team verified the original reference
collection. These procedures preserve the distinction between agreement
among model annotations and verification against the underlying
documents.

Requirements are mapped back to the comments whose requests they answer.
For a thread spanning several rounds, independent mappings retain agreed
comment–requirement links. A requirement introduced by a later follow-up
is not assigned retrospectively to an earlier comment. Repeated requests
can refer to the same requirement in several rounds, whereas an earlier
request that has already been satisfied is not automatically carried
into every follow-up. Consequently, the benchmark counts requirement
occurrences per eligible comment and round, rather than deduplicating
them across threads. Annotation and mapping records retain fingerprints
of their inputs, prompts, and model identities. Unchanged inputs reuse
saved annotations; altered inputs require a new record. This preserves
the connection between each reference requirement and the source version
used to establish it, including when a review package is reconstructed.

| Disposition | Count | Share | Needs facts |  Evidence target |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Disclosure change | 4,668 | 76.5% | 2,093 (44.8%) |  Amended filing with the required addition, edit, or removal |
| Explanation to staff | 1,075 | 17.6% | 805 (74.9%) |  Formal response with the requested explanation or analysis |
| Supporting material | 173 | 2.8% | 33 (19.1%) |  Submission containing the requested document, exhibit, or copy |
| Commitment | 183 | 3.0% | 149 (81.4%) |  Formal response with an explicit commitment to future action |
| Total | 6,099 | 100% | 3,080 (50.5%) |  Requirement-specific evidence in the designated deliverable |

Table 3. Requirement dispositions and evidence targets. Fact percentages
are within each disposition.

Verification follows the required deliverable: a reply claiming that a
filing was revised does not replace evidence in the amended filing
itself. Conversely, an explanation or a commitment is assessed in the
formal response, while a request for supporting material requires the
material to be supplied. Mixed comments retain separate evidence targets
for each constituent requirement.

### A.4. Scoring Eligibility and Corpus Coverage

A comment is scorable when it is detectable from the permitted record,
its annotation is usable, and at least one applicable requirement has
sufficient evidence. Company facts are scoped to the current comment and
round. Each must be required by an applicable requirement and supported
by a quotation from the bound response, revision, filing, or exhibit
evidence. Facts supported only in later rounds are withheld.
Requirements lacking necessary current-round fact evidence are excluded
before evaluation, removing 318 occurrences. The retained corpus
includes 3,080 fact-dependent requirements (50.5% of 6,099). This
annotation records what fulfillment requires, without asserting that
every marked fact is absent from every visible document.

Of 412 reconstructed review rounds in the main collection, 380 are
eligible and 32 remain in the exclusion records. A further 93 terminal
diagnostics are excluded: registration effectiveness and review closure
provide process context, without establishing that a filing contains no
remaining deficiencies. The final stream contains 3,012 scorable
comments and 6,099 requirement occurrences, using 378 distinct primary
versions and 1,311 distinct documents in permitted visible records.

The annual-report extension adds 2 tasks, four comments, and eight
requirement occurrences from an existing issuer’s Form 20-F review.
Package identity combines company identifier, form, fiscal period, and
original accession, distinguishing it from IPO review and other
reporting years. The first round includes an amended report and
certification exhibits; the second uses an explanatory response without
another amendment. Thus, reconstruction accommodates both revision and
explanation outcomes. This small extension adds document-type coverage
without supporting a separate characterization of annual-report review
performance.

All 380 tasks form one evaluation stream without training or validation
partitions, with identical reference inventories across configurations.
Figure [2](#acmlabel2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
counts whitespace-separated words per primary filing, excluding earlier
history: the median is 111,804 and the 90th percentile is 155,266. These
task-weighted counts differ from model tokens and the total volume of
visible material.

## Appendix B Task Environment and Interaction Protocol

The environment presents historical review rounds as Reviewer–Filer
interactions. A trusted host routes submissions, maintains authoritative
artifacts, and supplies bounded facts. Role-specific workspaces separate
source evidence, proposed revisions, and committed outcomes.

### B.1. Information Boundaries and Role Workspaces

Each task starts from the reviewed filing and the earlier records
permitted by its historical boundary
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")).
The materialized record includes primary text, section and printed-page
indexes, linked exhibits and attachments, and available image records.
Navigation metadata identifies source locations without supplying the
reference comments or marking which passages contain scored
deficiencies. The host retains current historical correspondence,
subsequent amendments, requirement annotations, and the complete fact
ledger.

Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.1. Information Boundaries and Role Workspaces ‣ Appendix B Task Environment and Interaction Protocol ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
summarizes access during an active task. Reviewer and Filer use separate
role contexts. Both can inspect the permitted record and the current
authoritative filing, while formal comments and responses provide the
exchange between them. Company questions and released answers enter only
the Filer’s private history; the Reviewer can assess information that
the Filer subsequently includes in its formal response or the revised
filing. Documents and exchange records preserve case history without
sharing private role conversations.

The record is read-only, and proposed edits are submitted separately
from the authoritative draft. Adapters receive a turn-specific workspace
and submission contract rather than access to the controller’s reference
files. Private fact-service diagnostics, including historical comment
identities used for matching, remain outside the acting agents’ inputs.
Current-task grading judgments are likewise withheld during execution.
The subsequent use of locked feedback for procedural evolution is
described in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Procedural Evolution ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

|  Record or artifact | Reviewer | Filer | Trusted host |
|----|----|----|----|
|  Permitted filing and earlier history | Read | Read | Selects sources |
|  Current draft and committed edits | Read | Propose edits | Validates and commits |
|  Generated review comments | Author | Read | Retains and routes |
|  Formal issuer responses | Read | Author | Retains and routes |
|  Company questions and released answers | Hidden | Private access | Serves scoped facts |
|  Current historical letters and amendments | Hidden | Hidden | Reference evidence |
|  Atomic requirements and complete fact ledger | Hidden | Hidden | Reference evidence |
|  Current-task grading judgments | Hidden | Hidden | Assesses final artifacts |

Table 4. Information access during a task. Private fact-service records
and current-task grading judgments remain separated from the public
exchange.

### B.2. Tools, Submissions, and Committed Artifacts

The built-in agents combine document reading with shell-based inspection
and file preparation. Text can be read by line range or printed-page
range, and linked images can be inspected separately from surrounding
extracted text. Section indexes and source paths support focused reading
across long filings. External frameworks retain their native tool loops
while using the same permitted records and submission contract. Their
measured resource usage is reported alongside nominal execution budgets
in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1. Experimental Setup ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

The initial Reviewer submission is a list of comments with stable
identifiers, an optional heading, a substantive request, a source
document, and a supporting quotation. Identifiers must be distinct, and
quotations must match a supplied document or current draft under the
controller’s source checks. Source quotations ground comment locations;
semantic validity is assessed separately. New comments introduced during
re-review follow the same contract and cannot reuse identifiers already
assigned in the case.

The Filer supplies exactly one response for each active comment,
choosing revised, explained, information_requested, or declined. Each
response identifies the comment and provides the formal reply;
information requests additionally contain explicit questions. Text edits
are separate transactions containing the text to find, its replacement,
and the comment identifiers motivating the change. The host applies a
replacement only when the target is unique in the current draft. It
first attempts exact matching, then a unique whitespace-normalized match
for eligible anchors. Missing or ambiguous targets are rejected with
reasons. Edits are applied in order against the evolving draft, making
their effects reproducible from the original text and committed
transaction records.

Tasks with supporting-document or image manifests also identify the
artifacts that may be changed. Supporting-text revisions name the
authorized document, its base hash, and the proposed text edits. Image
removal identifies a currently present asset and verifies its source
hash before changing its manifest state. Original source files remain
preserved. Directly altering a workspace copy or claiming that an
attachment was changed does not replace the corresponding committed
operation. These controls preserve the distinction between a proposed
action and the final deliverable evaluated.

### B.3. Bounded Company-Fact Acquisition

The fact service represents company information supported by the
historical record. It is accessed through a Filer information request
associated with an active generated comment. The trusted host matches
that concern to current-round reference comments and returns the
permitted facts associated with the matched concerns. It does not expose
those reference identifiers, the reference response, or the complete
fact ledger. The returned material is restricted by the source and
temporal eligibility rules in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4. Scoring Eligibility and Corpus Coverage ‣ Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

The service is therefore a bounded source of evidence, rather than an
unrestricted company question-answering system. A request can return no
material because no concern was linked or no releasable facts support
it. Such an answer describes service coverage, not the real company’s
knowledge or willingness to respond. Released facts may include the
company’s own positions, analyses, or commitments; they remain
attributable company statements rather than independent certification of
those claims.

Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ B.3. Bounded Company-Fact Acquisition ‣ Appendix B Task Environment and Interaction Protocol ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
shows how fact acquisition connects to revision. Supported edits and
non-request responses are committed even when other comments require
information. After the service returns, the Filer receives the updated
draft, released answers, retained responses, and edit acceptance or
rejection records. Finalization covers only the pending comment
identifiers, including those requiring correction of rejected edits;
previously committed work is retained. The Filer cannot issue another
information request within that finalization phase. Released answers
remain available in its private case history for later exchanges.

robot, source documents, marked-up drafts, and magnifiers to depict
discovery, response, and re-review. A gold private lane shows a human
company representative supplying documented facts and a robot committing
a revised filing with red before-text and green after-text. Accepted

loop, clock, and hourglass symbols mark resolution, another exchange,
deferred information, and the exchange limit. Validation, preservation
of final artifacts, and independent grading remain distinct

Figure 7. Illustrated interaction protocol. Reviewer and Filer exchange
grounded comments, responses, and revisions. Company facts remain

Re-review controls iteration, while independent grading assesses frozen
````
