````math
teal Filer robot, source documents, marked-up drafts, and magnifiers to
depict discovery, response, and re-review. A gold private lane shows a
human company representative supplying documented facts and a robot
committing a revised filing with red before-text and green after-text.
Accepted work is retained while pending responses are finalized.
Distinct check, loop, clock, and hourglass symbols mark resolution,
another exchange, deferred information, and the exchange limit.
Validation, preservation of final artifacts, and independent grading
remain distinct controls.

### B.4. Multi-Turn Control and Termination

The controller begins with Reviewer discovery, routes valid comments to
the Filer, and requests re-review after the responses and revisions are
committed. The Reviewer assigns every active concern one status:
resolved, unresolved, or awaiting_company_information, with a reason. It
can also introduce new grounded concerns. Unresolved concerns and valid
new comments form the next active set. Concerns awaiting company
information are retained as deferred work in the case record, rather
than erased from the final account of outstanding obligations. Statuses
and reasons are recorded with their exchange for subsequent inspection.

The main experiments permit at most three review–revision exchanges,
with the role-invocation budgets specified in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1. Experimental Setup ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").
A fact request and its finalization belong to the same exchange.
Execution ends when discovery produces no valid comments, no actionable
concerns remain after re-review, or the exchange limit is reached. A
completed interaction can therefore retain deferred or unresolved
concerns. The independent evaluator assesses the frozen final artifacts
against the eligible reference requirements; the acting Reviewer’s
decision to close a concern does not determine its benchmark score.

The host validates submission structure, active-identifier coverage,
source quotations, and task and draft integrity before advancing a turn.
A saved artifact can proceed at an execution limit only after host
validation. Invalid or failed turns retain explicit failure states.
Accepted and rejected edits, released facts, remaining concerns, final
documents, and responses are preserved for assessment.
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
defines execution and fulfillment accounting.

## Appendix C Agent Prompts

FilingLoop separates shared execution instructions, fixed role
instructions, and learned procedural guidance. The shared instructions
require evidence for company claims, restrict work to authorized files,
and treat documents and tool outputs as data rather than instructions.
The role prompt specifies the review or revision objective and its
submission contract. Each invocation also receives a task description
identifying the mode, visible record, active comments, and output file.
Both variants begin with identical fixed instructions and empty learned
guidance. Evolving appends a role-specific procedure frozen for the
current batch; the fixed instructions, task schema, and evidence
permissions retain precedence over that procedure.

The boxes below reproduce selected prompt passages, grouped by
operational stage and reflowed for readability. Repeated tool-navigation
instructions and conditional image and attachment operations are omitted
from the displays; the complete shared, Reviewer, Filer, and Skill
Editor source prompts accompany the implementation.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Task Environment and Interaction Protocol ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
defines the corresponding workspace and artifact contracts, and
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Procedural Evolution ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
describes when learned guidance can change.

### C.1. Reviewer Prompt

The Reviewer uses the same role prompt for initial discovery and
subsequent re-review, with the task mode selecting the relevant
instructions. Discovery starts from the permitted filing rather than a
supplied list of reference deficiencies. The prompt therefore combines
filing-wide coverage with materiality and evidence checks: inspecting a
section does not itself justify issuing a comment. It also distinguishes
overlapping requests from separate obligations within a compound
comment, preserving the latter for revision.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each generated comment links a requested action to a source passage
through id, heading, comment, document, and quote. The source anchor
supports verification of the concern’s location without supplying the
hidden reference answer. During re-review, the Reviewer receives formal
responses and committed artifacts, while the Filer’s private company
questions and answers remain outside its context. The instructions below
require inspection of the deliverable itself and separate actionable
corrections from obligations awaiting unavailable facts.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The three statuses serve different purposes. resolved closes a concern
in the interaction; unresolved identifies work that can still proceed;
and awaiting_company_information preserves a deferred obligation. A
single missing fact must not defer other supported corrections in the
same comment. The statuses and new_comments fields in rereview.json
preserve these decisions for the controller. Final benchmark credit
remains determined by the independent assessment of the frozen
artifacts.

This separation is especially important for compound requests: a
response may supply a satisfactory explanation while leaving a requested
filing amendment incomplete. Re-review must track which obligation was
fulfilled in which artifact, rather than treating a persuasive letter as
evidence that all associated document changes were committed.

### C.2. Filer Prompt

The Filer acts as issuer counsel and must produce both a formal response
and the requested document changes. Its prompt distinguishes four
response actions so that a defensible explanation, a supported revision,
a request for missing facts, and an inapplicable concern remain explicit
choices. Company answers are attributable evidence about the issuer’s
facts and positions. An empty service response does not establish that
the real company lacks the requested information or authorize a
fabricated answer.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The finalization instructions preserve progress across the
fact-acquisition boundary. Supported changes can be committed before
every fact is available; the follow-up receives the updated draft and
only the remaining comment identifiers. This prevents an information
request from blocking unrelated work and prevents previously accepted
edits from being applied twice. Released answers remain in a private,
exchange-dated case history so that later turns can reuse evidence
without repeating the same question.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Filer submits response.json with responses and edits; a response
names the comment and action, while each edit contains find, replace,
and comment_ids. Separating the letter from the edit transactions makes
the requested deliverable explicit. The final consistency check then
extends beyond the edited paragraph: a revised claim or numerical
disclosure must agree with surviving statements elsewhere in the filing.
The agent’s verification.json records its own checks, whereas host
acceptance establishes structural validity and independent evaluation
determines requirement fulfillment.

### C.3. Skill Editor Prompt

The Skill Editor operates between completed batches rather than within a
scored case. It is invoked separately for Reviewer and Filer. Its JSON
payload specifies role, skill_name, fixed_base_instructions,
current_skill, and completed_batch_feedback. The feedback records
discovered concerns, applicable requirements, fulfillment judgments,
supporting quotations, and reasons. These inputs allow the editor to
convert a recurring failure into a reusable procedure while preserving
the distinction between review coverage and revision quality. The full
editor instruction is reproduced below.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The output is a JSON decision with either action=no_change and a
rationale, or action=propose, a rationale, and skill_markdown. A
proposed skill includes the expected name, description, and role
metadata. Retaining the current skill is an explicit valid decision; the
suggested length is advisory. The editor changes procedural text while
model weights, fixed role instructions, evidence access, and scoring
rules remain fixed. Accepted guidance becomes available only to later
cases, after the supplying batch’s scores have been locked.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Procedural Evolution ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
specifies the validation and update schedule.

Role-specific editing connects each procedure to the agent’s
responsibility. Reviewer guidance can organize evidence search and
closure checks; Filer guidance can organize fact acquisition, response
coverage, and consistency verification. The transferable output is a
procedure for performing those operations. Company assertions still
require evidence from the new case’s permitted record or released
answers, even when prior feedback motivated the procedure used to
investigate them.

## Appendix D Procedural Evolution

FilingLoop adapts the procedures used to investigate and resolve
disclosure concerns. The learned state consists of two instruction
documents, one for Reviewer and one for Filer. Model weights, fixed role
instructions, tools, evidence access, and evaluation rules remain
unchanged. Both variants begin with empty learned guidance; only
Evolving updates these documents between completed batches.
Figure [8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ D.1. Role-Specific Guidance ‣ Appendix D Procedural Evolution ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
shows the boundary between performing a task and learning from its
locked outcome.

### D.1. Role-Specific Guidance

Each learned skill is a Markdown instruction document with YAML metadata
specifying its name, description, and target role. The body expresses
reusable actions, evidence checks, and stopping conditions. Reviewer
guidance can organize filing coverage, distinguish an actual deficiency
from an already answered question, or require verification of every
obligation in a compound comment. Filer guidance can organize supported
edits, targeted fact requests, and checks for contradictory statements
elsewhere in the draft. These examples describe the kinds of procedures
the representation supports, rather than introducing additional company
information into an active case.

The editor receives the fixed instructions, current role skill, and
feedback from the completed Evolving batch. Feedback includes the
reference concern, its discovery outcome, applicable requirements,
fulfillment judgments, supporting quotations, and reasons. This
distinguishes a missed concern from a discovered concern whose requested
amendment was never committed. The editor can therefore address a
failure at the relevant stage instead of merely encouraging a longer
comment letter or response. Its prompt and decision schema are
reproduced in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3. Skill Editor Prompt ‣ Appendix C Agent Prompts ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

The fixed role prompt takes precedence over learned guidance. Within a
case, agents may revise documents and retain their own task history, but
they cannot rewrite the frozen skill. Across cases, only the validated
procedural text is transferred. A previous company’s amount, contract
term, or response does not become evidence for another issuer. Current
assertions still need support from the new task’s permitted documents or
released company facts.

![Illustrated Reviewer and Filer robots use frozen role playbooks. A
padlock and assessment checklist denote locked first-pass outcomes. A
fictional research editor and robot revise two procedural books, and
later tasks receive validated guidance with the same models and tools.
Arrows point forward without returning to scored
tasks.](2610.37905v1/filingloop_evolution_protocol.png)

Figure 8. Procedural evolution across batches. Skills remain frozen
during execution. Locked Evolving outcomes inform validated role updates
used only by subsequent tasks; Fixed guidance remains
unchanged.Illustrated Reviewer and Filer robots use frozen role
playbooks. A padlock and assessment checklist denote locked first-pass
outcomes. A fictional research editor and robot revise two procedural
books, and later tasks receive validated guidance with the same models
and tools. Arrows point forward without returning to scored tasks.

### D.2. Update Validation

For each role, the editor returns either no_change with a rationale or
propose with a rationale and a complete replacement skill. Validation
checks the decision fields, nonempty text, valid YAML, expected skill
name, and consistency of any declared role metadata. The skill format
accepts instruction metadata and a nonempty body; unfinished markers and
ambiguous duplicate YAML keys are rejected. The editor is instructed to
produce procedural prose rather than executable code or additional
permissions.

Content checks reject known instance identifiers, company names and
CIKs, and private source paths from the evaluation plan. They also
reject exact copies of sufficiently long reference comments or
requirement descriptions from the supplied feedback. These checks
accompany the prompt’s prohibition on memorizing company facts, dates,
amounts, and reference answers. Their purpose is to keep the
transferable artifact focused on procedure; the limits of textual checks
are discussed in
Appendix [I.2](#A9.SS2 "I.2. Evaluator Validity and Online Adaptation ‣ Appendix I Limitations and Responsible Data Use ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

An invalid proposal receives the validation error and a request to
repair the complete document or retain the current skill. The
implementation allows at most three proposal attempts per role. If no
valid replacement is obtained, the existing skill is retained. The
approximately 1,500-token length target is advisory: longer valid skills
are neither rejected nor truncated solely for exceeding it. The retained
text, decision, rationale, and before/after hashes identify exactly
which procedure becomes available to later tasks.

Validation checks the structure and permitted content of a proposed
skill. A valid replacement enters the next batch without a held-out
performance-selection stage or replay of completed cases. Its effect is
measured through first-pass outcomes on the later tasks that actually
use it. This schedule keeps feedback tied to already locked outcomes
while preserving the fixed evidence permissions and role instructions
under which subsequent filings are investigated and revised.

### D.3. Online Update Schedule

Tasks are ordered by a seeded company permutation and chronological
review rounds within each company. The stream interleaves companies and
forms batches of at most 16 tasks, with no company repeated within a
batch. For batch $`b`$, let $`S_{R}^{(b)}`$ and $`S_{F}^{(b)}`$ denote
the two frozen skills. All tasks in the batch use these versions, and
updates wait for the whole paired batch to complete assessment
regardless of asynchronous completion order.

After the paired batch has completed assessment, the controller locks
its first-pass scores and builds feedback from the Evolving outcomes.
The editor then produces $`S_{R}^{(b+1)}`$ and $`S_{F}^{(b+1)}`$,
subject to the checks above. Only not-yet-started tasks can use the
resulting guidance. Fixed retains empty learned skills throughout, and
its outcomes do not enter the Evolving editor’s feedback. If a batch is
incompletely assessed, it supplies no update; there is no unused editor
call after the final batch.

The saved batch record links its task identifiers, frozen policy hash,
feedback boundary, locked scores, and accepted next policy. Continuation
restores these records rather than generating a second update from the
same completed batch. Earlier rounds of an issuer can inform procedures
used on its later rounds, but the resulting score remains an online
adaptation measurement. It does not treat successive rounds from the
same company as independent evidence of transfer to previously unseen
issuers.

## Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting

This appendix defines the accuracy, completion, and resource measures in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
and the efficiency comparisons in
Section [4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6. Resource Efficiency (RQ3) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").
Let $`\mathcal{T}`$ be the evaluated task set. For task
$`t\in\mathcal{T}`$, let $`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$ contain its scorable
comments and $`\mathcal{U}_{ti}`$ the eligible requirements of comment
$`i`$, indexed by $`j`$. The binary indicators $`d_{ti}`$ and
$`b_{tij}`$ denote comment discovery and requirement fulfillment,
respectively. Eligibility is fixed before execution, so undiscovered
concerns remain in the system denominators. All accuracies below are
fractions reported as percentages; harm audits are reported separately
from resolution accuracy.

### E.1. Accuracy Definitions and Reporting Scopes

Let $`s\in\{A,R,F\}`$ denote the complete system, Reviewer, or Filer.
System and Reviewer outcomes cover all scorable reference comments,
$`\mathcal{C}_{t}^{A}=\mathcal{C}_{t}^{R}=\mathcal{C}_{t}`$. For the
paired Filer diagnostics, let $`\mathcal{D}_{t}^{0}`$ be the reference
comments assigned to Filer by the Fixed variant, and set
$`\mathcal{C}_{t}^{F}=\mathcal{D}_{t}^{0}`$ in both variants. The
eligible requirement set is
$`\mathcal{E}_{t}^{s}=\{(i,j):i\in\mathcal{C}_{t}^{s},j\in\mathcal{U}_{ti}\}`$.
For an eligible requirement, define $`z_{tij}^{A}=d_{ti}b_{tij}`$,
$`z_{tij}^{R}=d_{ti}`$, and $`z_{tij}^{F}=b_{tij}`$. Thus the system
requires both discovery and fulfillment, Reviewer measures discovery,
and Filer measures fulfillment on its shared conditional target pool,
with both variants assessed on identical assigned requirements for this
diagnostic. Both numerators include only verdicts linked to the Fixed
pool’s reference comment IDs; additional Evolving discoveries remain in
the system score. This is a post-hoc scoring restriction: each Filer
responds to its own Reviewer, retaining the interaction history that
produced its final artifacts.

Reviewer requirement credit inherits the matching decision for the
parent comment; it does not imply that the agent separately identified
every atomic requirement. Fulfillment is checked in the deliverable
requested by the requirement: a filing amendment must appear in the
final filing, whereas an explanation or commitment must appear in the
appropriate response. A reply asserting that an amendment was made
cannot substitute for the amendment. The role rows describe stages of
the same interaction, so their successful and eligible counts are never
added to obtain the system’s accuracy.

Table [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ E.1. Accuracy Definitions and Reporting Scopes ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
specifies the aggregate denominators. System and Reviewer retain the
full reference collection for both variants. Filer retains the same
Fixed target pool, even when Evolving discovers additional concerns.
This makes corresponding role percentages comparable without allowing a
change in target coverage to change the diagnostic’s denominator. Tasks
with no assigned Filer requirements are excluded from its conditional
Task Accuracy; companies enter its Company Accuracy only when they have
at least one nonempty scoped target.

|  Reporting scope                   | Requirements | Comments | Tasks | Companies |
|------------------------------------|--------------|----------|-------|-----------|
|  System and Reviewer               | 6,099        | 3,012    | 380   | 96        |
|  Filer (shared Fixed target pool)  | 2,162        | 983      | 283   | 95        |

Table 5. Accuracy denominators. Both variants use the same scoped
targets.

Requirement Accuracy. This metric pools successful requirement checks
across tasks:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (4) |  |
``` math
\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{req}}(s)=\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{t}^{s}}z_{tij}^{s}}{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\mathcal{E}_{t}^{s}|}.
``` |  |

Each requirement occurrence has equal weight, including those whose
parent comments were not discovered. Partial resolution contributes
credit for satisfied requirements while retaining the remaining
obligations in the denominator. Pooling requirement checks avoids
weighting tasks equally when their numbers of applicable requirements
differ substantially. Requirements can share evidence or logical
prerequisites; equal weighting counts annotated obligations rather than
independent failure causes.

Comment Accuracy. A comment passes only if all its applicable
requirements pass. Writing
$`w_{ti}^{s}=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{U}_{ti}}z_{tij}^{s}`$, we obtain

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (5) |  |
``` math
\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{comment}}(s)=\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{t}^{s}}w_{ti}^{s}}{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\mathcal{C}_{t}^{s}|}.
``` |  |

Each comment has equal weight, regardless of its requirement count.
Reviewer must discover the comment, Filer must fulfill its assigned
requirements, and the system requires both. Unlike Requirement Accuracy,
Comment Accuracy withholds credit when even one obligation in a compound
request remains unsatisfied in the final deliverables.

Task Accuracy. Let $`\mathcal{T}_{s}^{+}`$ contain tasks with known,
nonempty scoped requirement sets. Set $`p_{t}^{s}=1`$ only when the
required assessment is complete and every requirement in
$`\mathcal{E}_{t}^{s}`$ passes; otherwise set $`p_{t}^{s}=0`$. Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (6) |  |
``` math
\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{task}}(s)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{s}^{+}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{s}^{+}}p_{t}^{s}.
``` |  |

Task success requires complete discovery for Reviewer, complete
fulfillment of assigned requirements for Filer, and both for the system.
Partial completion earns no fractional credit; tasks with empty Filer
assignments are excluded from conditional accuracy.

Company Accuracy. Let $`\mathcal{G}_{s}^{+}`$ contain companies with at
least one nonempty scoped target. Set $`p_{c}^{s}=1`$ only when all
applicable requirements across company $`c`$’s tasks pass and all
required task assessments are complete; otherwise set $`p_{c}^{s}=0`$.
Company Accuracy is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (7) |  |
``` math
\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{company}}(s)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{s}^{+}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{G}_{s}^{+}}p_{c}^{s}.
``` |  |

Each eligible company receives one outcome covering all its review
rounds. One failed requirement prevents a company pass, and an unknown
task target prevents certification of complete success. Passing selected
rounds is insufficient to establish resolution of the company’s full set
of disclosure obligations.

Counts and comparisons. Parentheses in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
show successful/eligible integer counts; percentages are rounded after
aggregation. Empty aggregate target sets yield undefined accuracy with
reported coverage. Percentage-point gains in
Figure [5](#acmlabel5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.5. Effect of Procedural Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
subtract displayed accuracies, whereas relative gains in fulfilled
requirements and resolved comments use their underlying integer counts
before percentage rounding.

### E.2. Task Completion and Harm Audits

Task completion. Completion measures execution reliability over all 380
scheduled tasks, independently of the conditional Filer accuracy
denominator. Joint completion requires a finished interaction and
assessment; role completion requires every recorded invocation in the
retained episode to return an accepted response or host-validated
submission. Unneeded phases are not counted as executed invocations. A
completed interaction can still retain unresolved concerns or deferred
requests, because completion records process termination while accuracy
records fulfillment of the disclosure obligations.

Failed or unassessed cases receive no end-to-end accuracy credit, and
their known targets remain in the system denominators. Task and Company
Accuracy also require complete assessment, preventing a method from
benefiting when difficult cases fail to finish. Execution status,
assessment coverage, and partial artifacts distinguish process failure
from unmet disclosure requirements in an assessed submission.

Harm audits. The evaluator records unfounded additional comments,
comments containing contradicted company assertions, and tasks with
harmful filing changes. Harmful changes introduce unsupported claims or
contradictions, or damage supported disclosure; an unresolved original
request alone is not harm. The harmful-revision rate is the fraction of
tasks with a completed edit audit that contain at least one harmful
filing change. Edit-audit coverage is the fraction of all scheduled
tasks with such an audit; unaudited tasks are not counted as harm-free.
Additional concerns are checked against permitted evidence; lacking a
historical match does not itself establish an unfounded request.
Insufficient support and contradiction remain distinct outcomes. Audit
counts supplement the four accuracies without being subtracted from
them, and assessment coverage distinguishes unassessed changes from
changes that were checked and found to contain no harmful modifications.

### E.3. Resource Usage and Efficiency

Tokens and cost. Input and Output in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
are cumulative token totals over all scheduled tasks, reported in
millions. Input includes cache-read and cache-write usage; Output
includes reasoning tokens. API cost is calculated from recorded usage
and the saved price schedule, including agent execution, compaction,
fact matching, assessment, applicable recovery calls, and skill updates.
Role rows contain usage attributed to that role; shared services and
unassigned usage remain in the system total. System cost can therefore
exceed the sum of the displayed Reviewer and Filer costs, and
comparisons include the shared services required to produce the scored
outcomes as well as the agents’ own model calls. The amounts are
calculated from logged usage and saved prices rather than reconciled
invoice totals.

Agent time. For role $`s\in\{R,F\}`$, let $`\Delta_{tsk}`$ be the
recorded duration in hours of invocation $`k`$ on task $`t`$. Cumulative
Agent hours and mean minutes per scheduled task are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (8) |  |
``` math
T_{s}=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{k}\Delta_{tsk},\qquad T_{A}=T_{R}+T_{F},\qquad\overline{T}_{s}=\frac{60T_{s}}{|\mathcal{T}|}.
``` |  |

Invocation timers include model calls, tools, and compaction, while
independent assessment and gaps between stopping and restarting are
excluded. Concurrent tasks each contribute their own execution duration,
so the sum measures cumulative work rather than elapsed experiment time.
The average uses all 380 scheduled tasks, including unfinished tasks and
tasks with no discovered concerns. For FilingLoop, both total and
average system times equal the sums of the corresponding role values.
Reported durations retain recorded interrupted segments where available;
missing durations are not imputed or replaced by elapsed run intervals.

Efficiency ratios. Let $`K`$ be total system cost and
$`N_{\mathrm{met}}`$ the number of fulfilled reference requirements.
Cost per task is $`K/|\mathcal{T}|`$, requirements fulfilled per \$100
is $`100N_{\mathrm{met}}/K`$, and requirements fulfilled per Agent hour
is $`N_{\mathrm{met}}/T_{A}`$. Unit cost per fulfilled requirement is
$`K/N_{\mathrm{met}}`$, defined when at least one requirement is
fulfilled.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.6. Resource Efficiency (RQ3) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
uses the resource totals displayed in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
to calculate these ratios. This common accounting basis connects
expenditure to successful disclosure corrections while preserving the
distinction between total cost, cumulative Agent work, and the number of
tasks scheduled for evaluation.

## Appendix F Experimental Configuration and Reproducibility

This section records the settings shared by the comparisons and the
artifacts needed to reproduce their execution and analysis.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
specifies all eight framework–backbone configurations; the common task,
interaction, and update settings are summarized below. Metric formulas
and resource accounting follow
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

### F.1. Models, Inference, and Execution Settings

The same backbone serves Reviewer and Filer within each configuration.
FilingLoop–Fixed, FilingLoop–Evolving, Codex, and one mini-SWE-agent
configuration use gpt-6.1-sol. The other mini-SWE-agent configurations
use claude-opus-5.5, gemini-4-argon, and deepseek-v4.1-flash; Claude
Code uses claude-opus-5.5. The reference default reasoning effort is
high. Provider-specific inference options and resolved model identifiers
accompany each request; the common effort label does not equate internal
computation across the different backbones used in the comparison.
Measured token use, cost, and execution time characterize the
computational effort of each configuration.

| Setting |  Configuration |
|----|----|
| Evaluation population |  380 tasks, 96 companies; 378 registration and 2 annual-report tasks |
| Task order |  Seed 0; interleaved companies, chronological rounds within each company |
| Update batches |  At most 16 tasks; no repeated company in the same batch |
| Concurrent execution |  Up to 16 tasks; policies frozen throughout each update batch |
| Interaction budget |  At most 3 exchanges; 100 reference steps per role invocation |
| Reasoning effort |  high by default; provider options retained in request records |
| Evaluation services |  gpt-6.1-sol for grading, fact matching, and skill editing |
| Initial learned guidance |  Empty for both roles in Fixed and Evolving |
| Learning boundary |  Locked completed-batch feedback; updated skills apply only to later tasks |
| Main outcome convention |  One first-pass outcome per task; strict all-requirements task/company success |

Table 6. Shared settings for the reported evaluation.

The independent evaluator uses gpt-6.1-sol for matching, requirement
fulfillment, and harm assessment. The same model performs fact matching
and skill editing. The evaluator underwent manual review; all
configurations use the same grading model, prompts, and artifact checks.
Acting agents receive mechanical submission feedback during their turns
but no current-task grading judgments. The execution manifest binds the
chosen models, inference settings, source fingerprints, and runtime
configuration to the task plan, keeping later configuration changes
separate from the recorded comparison.

### F.2. Baseline Adapters and Common Contracts

Every framework receives separate Reviewer and Filer workspaces with the
same permitted source records and turn-specific artifact contract. The
host routes comments, releases bounded company facts to Filer, commits
valid edits, and supplies the current draft for re-review. Reference
comments, requirement annotations, unreleased company facts, and grading
results are not available to the acting baseline. Matching and final
assessment operate on the resulting artifacts through the common
evaluator.

FilingLoop supplies its document-reading and shell tools, while
mini-SWE-agent retains its shell-based interaction loop. Codex and
Claude Code retain their native file, shell, session, and compaction
behavior through role adapters. Their execution environments restrict
access to the authorized workspace; inference credentials are kept
outside the task materials. Personal plugins, unrelated repository
instructions, and another role’s private context do not become
additional task inputs through the adapter.

The reference budget is 100 steps per role invocation, including
follow-up phases, with at most three review–revision exchanges. A
FilingLoop step is one model response and its resulting tool calls.
Native frameworks count and manage execution differently, so the nominal
allocation does not establish equal internal steps or equal inference
expenditure. The measured tokens, cost, and cumulative Agent time in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
expose these differences alongside the shared evidence and submission
conditions.

### F.3. Execution Records and Continuation

The task plan fixes the eligible corpus, company order, within-company
chronology, and source fingerprints. Batch policy snapshots record the
two skills before tasks start. Per-task records retain role submissions,
edit acceptance or rejection, released facts, final artifacts, evaluator
judgments, and usage. Locked results and update records connect the
scored case to the procedure available to subsequent tasks, preserving
both the outcome and its position in the adaptation stream.

Continuation uses the saved task and policy state. Completed submissions
can proceed to unfinished assessment, and recorded model responses can
be reused only when their request and source identity match. Restored
policy snapshots prevent repeated editing of the same completed batch.
The reported stream does not replace a scored attempt with a later
replay under improved guidance. Failed cases retain their known
reference targets under the accounting in
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2. Task Completion and Harm Audits ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

Usage records distinguish role execution from shared services and retain
the price schedule used for cost calculation. Invocation timers measure
Agent work, while task and run timestamps separately describe elapsed
time. This distinction matters under concurrent execution: overlapping
tasks can reduce elapsed duration without reducing their cumulative
model or tool work. Recovered artifacts preserve their original identity
rather than being counted as newly generated responses.

### F.4. Reproducing the Reported Analyses

Reproduction starts from the frozen task plan, source records, role
prompts, inference settings, and batch policies. The task identifiers
and source fingerprints determine the evaluated population; workspace
materialization then enforces the historical boundary described in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1. Information Boundaries and Role Workspaces ‣ Appendix B Task Environment and Interaction Protocol ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").
Following the same company order is necessary for Evolving because a
task’s policy depends on the completed batches before it, not solely on
its own filing and model configuration.

The manuscript analysis takes tables/main_results.tex as the numeric
source. The script scripts/build_rq_analysis.py checks the displayed
accuracies against successful/eligible counts and derives the RQ
summaries. The script scripts/build_evolution_effects.py regenerates
Figure [5](#acmlabel5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.5. Effect of Procedural Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision"),
and scripts/build_appendix_extended.py regenerates the additional
accounting in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Extended Results and Analyses ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").
These operations use saved numbers without model inference or changes to
the underlying judgments. The paper is compiled with pdfLaTeX and TeX
Live 2026 through build.sh; editable figure sources and source hashes
accompany the exported publication figures.

## Appendix G Extended Results and Analyses

We extend the main comparison through accounting of completed tasks,
discovery and fulfillment, and attributed resources. All quantities
below derive from the successful/eligible counts and resource totals in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision"),
using the evaluated population and reporting scopes formally defined in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

### G.1. Completion and Resolution Granularity

Both FilingLoop variants complete 379 of 380 scheduled tasks. Among
those completed tasks, 364 in Fixed and 360 in Evolving do not pass
every requirement. Across all eight configurations, this count lies
between 360 and 364 tasks. The dominant gap is therefore between a
finished interaction and complete disclosure resolution. Improving
execution completion alone would leave most of these substantive
failures in place under the strict task metric.

Granularity also changes the ordering of methods. Evolving fulfills
1,705 requirements and resolves 625 comments, the largest counts in the
comparison, while mini-SWE-agent/Opus completes 20 fully successful
tasks versus Evolving’s 19. Company-level success is stricter still:
Evolving passes two companies, Fixed one, and the external
configurations none. These outcomes favor tracking all outstanding
obligations within a review, including those left after many
individually successful edits, rather than using the number of completed
actions as the stopping condition for a task or company review history.

### G.2. Discovery and Fulfillment Bottlenecks

Figure [9](#A7.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ G.2. Discovery and Fulfillment Bottlenecks ‣ Appendix G Extended Results and Analyses ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")(a–b)
partitions each reference inventory into three disjoint groups:
undiscovered items, discovered but unfulfilled items, and fulfilled
items. Requirement discovery inherits the parent-comment match, as in
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1. Accuracy Definitions and Reporting Scopes ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Metrics and Accounting ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision");
a comment enters the fulfilled group only when all its requirements
pass. For either counting level, the identity is
$`N_{\mathrm{total}}=N_{\mathrm{missed}}+N_{\mathrm{open}}+N_{\mathrm{met}}`$.
This exposes the work excluded from a conditional Filer accuracy without
changing any of the system denominators.

![Three panels compare Fixed and Evolving with stacked bars.
Requirements and comments are partitioned into missed, open, and met
counts. A third panel partitions dollar cost into Reviewer, Filer, and
shared usage. Reviewer and Filer character icons accompany the
resolution panels.](2610.37905v1/filingloop_extended_accounting.png)

Figure 9. Resolution and resource accounting. Missed denotes
undiscovered reference items; Open denotes discovered but unfulfilled
items. Cost separates attributed roles from shared services. All values
derive from
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").Three
panels compare Fixed and Evolving with stacked bars. Requirements and
comments are partitioned into missed, open, and met counts. A third
panel partitions dollar cost into Reviewer, Filer, and shared usage.
Reviewer and Filer character icons accompany the resolution panels.

Fixed leaves 3,937 requirements undiscovered and 681 discovered but
unfulfilled. Evolving reduces these counts to 3,851 and 543,
respectively. At comment level, the corresponding groups change from
2,029 missed and 474 open comments to 1,990 and 397. Undiscovered items
account for 87.6% of Evolving’s remaining unfulfilled requirements and
83.4% of its unresolved reference comments. The residual error is thus
concentrated in concerns that never reach the revision workflow. Broader
Reviewer search must bring these omissions into the interaction before
targeted revisions and company-fact requests can address their
disclosure requirements.

The discovered requirement count rises by 86 while the discovered but
unfulfilled count falls by 138, giving the aggregate gain of
$`86+138=224`$ fulfilled requirements. The comment-level accounting is
$`39+77=116`$ additional resolved comments. These are net count
identities; they do not identify which individual requirements changed
state or assign causal contributions to discovery and revision. They
also explain why conditional Filer accuracy should be read alongside
Reviewer coverage: successful revision of assigned concerns cannot
resolve omissions that never enter that scope.

### G.3. Outcome Gains and Incremental Expenditure

Evolving adds \$139.08 and 14.32 recorded Agent hours over Fixed across
the complete stream. Dividing these increments by the additional
successful outcomes gives \$0.62 per extra fulfilled requirement and
\$1.20 per extra fully resolved comment. The time increment is 3.84
Agent minutes per additional fulfilled requirement. These stream-level
ratios include the resources of role execution and shared services under
the same accounting used for the two system totals.

The improvement also increases output per unit of total expenditure.
Requirements fulfilled per \$100 rise from 62.2 to 67.7, and
requirements per recorded Agent hour rise from 3.25 to 3.63
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.6. Resource Efficiency (RQ3) ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")).
Meanwhile, mean minutes per scheduled task rise from 71.85 to 74.11. The
extra work can therefore increase time per task while decreasing cost
per successful requirement. For disclosure agents, a useful optimization
target combines the cost of a task with the obligations actually
resolved by its final documents and responses.

separates resources attributed to Reviewer and Filer from the residual
shared component. Shared cost is \$495.34 for Fixed and \$539.92 for
Evolving, or 20.8% and 21.4% of their respective system totals. It
includes services that are not assigned to either role, such as
assessment, fact matching, and skill editing where applicable.
Figure [9](#A7.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ G.2. Discovery and Fulfillment Bottlenecks ‣ Appendix G Extended Results and Analyses ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")(c)
visualizes this decomposition without treating the entire shared
component as the cost of evolution.

|---------------------|----------|----------|--------|----------|----------|--------|
|  Resource           | Reviewer | Filer    | Shared | Reviewer | Filer    | Shared |
|  Input tokens (M)   | 3,041.21 | 2,848.36 | 209.02 | 3,126.36 | 3,076.23 | 229.92 |
|  Output tokens (M)  | 15.47    | 16.47    | 3.65   | 16.17    | 17.54    | 4.19   |

subtract the two role rows from the system total.

The additional \$139.08 consists of \$41.20 in Reviewer-attributed
usage, \$53.30 in Filer-attributed usage, and \$44.58 in shared usage.
The resource difference is distributed across the workflow rather than
confined to the editor call. Systems that learn reusable review
procedures must budget for applying them and assessing their resulting
artifacts as well as for producing the procedure itself. Cumulative
Agent hours remain a separate measure: they sum recorded role execution
and do not include independent assessment time.

## Appendix H Case Studies and Failure Analysis

We examine three evidence-linked cases covering successful resolution,
partial fulfillment of a compound request, and procedural transfer to a
later task. Each example follows a selected reference concern through
the generated comment, relevant interaction, committed artifacts, and
independent requirement judgments. The figures condense the interaction
wording while retaining its numerical evidence and document targets. A
requirement may call for a filing amendment, an explanation to Staff, or
a commitment in a formal reply; the assessment checks the corresponding
deliverable. These concern-level outcomes remain distinct from the
status of a broader agent comment or the success of the complete review
task, which may include additional requests for company information and
further amendments.

### H.1. Evidence-Grounded Disclosure Resolution

The first case concerns acquisition contributions to 2019 revenue growth
(reference concern r01:c09). The reviewed draft reports a \$1,501.3
million revenue increase but does not separately quantify the
contributions at issue. Reviewer comment R3 asks for acquisition effects
within a broader analysis of revenue and expense drivers. Filer requests
acquired-business revenue and growth contributions, and the company-fact
service releases two relevant facts: Pacific Union contributed \$362.6
million, or 15% of 2019 revenue, while the revenue increase attributable
to Paragon was less than 5% of company revenue in 2019 or any other
period.
Figure [10](#A8.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ H.1. Evidence-Grounded Disclosure Resolution ‣ Appendix H Case Studies and Failure Analysis ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
connects these facts to the two required deliverables.

![Four illustrated stages show Reviewer identifying an acquisition
revenue gap, Filer requesting facts, a company service returning Pacific
Union and Paragon contributions, and Filer committing a revision and
reply. The final assessment links each of two fulfilled requirements to
its artifact.](2610.37905v1/filingloop_case_resolution.png)

Figure 10. Evidence-grounded resolution of an acquisition disclosure
concern. Scoped company facts enter the filing and formal reply,
satisfying both selected requirements. Broader requests in agent comment
R3 remain deferred.Four illustrated stages show Reviewer identifying an
acquisition revenue gap, Filer requesting facts, a company service
returning Pacific Union and Paragon contributions, and Filer committing
a revision and reply. The final assessment links each of two fulfilled
requirements to its artifact.

Outcome and interpretation. Both selected requirements pass. The page-77
revenue discussion states Pacific Union’s dollar contribution and share
of revenue, satisfying the filing-amendment requirement. The formal
reply supplies Paragon’s relative contribution, providing the basis for
its earlier omission. Pacific Union’s full-year revenue contribution is
not treated as its incremental contribution to growth: the reply
preserves that distinction and identifies the broader decomposition
still requiring company information. The selected concern is therefore
resolved even though R3 retains other deferred requests. This case shows
why a useful disclosure agent must route each supported fact to its
required artifact and preserve the scope of what that fact establishes.
Acquiring the right number is one step; incorporating it into the filing
and the appropriate explanation is what fulfills the disclosure
obligation.

### H.2. Compound Requirements and Failure Localization

The second case concerns Evolus’s amended purchase agreement (reference
concern r03:c07). A \$43.1 million estimated value of revised
obligations and a promissory note does not identify the underlying
contractual cash amounts. Reviewer R3 requests payment obligations and
the note principal. The released company facts include an approximately
\$9.2 million approval-triggered upfront payment, a \$20.0 million note,
its material terms, and reasons for withholding exact royalty rates. The
company states that precise rates are not material to investors and that
disclosure would reveal cost and margin benchmarks to negotiating
counterparties. Thus, both the numerical amendments and the supporting
confidentiality explanation have evidence available to Filer.

Outcome and interpretation. Three of five eligible requirements pass.
The filing corrects the amounts and note terms; the reply commits to
withdrawing their confidentiality claims. However, retaining approximate
royalty rates requires the separate Staff explanation. Its omission
leaves both that justification and the selected disclosure alternative
incomplete.
Figure [11](#A8.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ H.2. Compound Requirements and Failure Localization ‣ Appendix H Case Studies and Failure Analysis ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
links the two failed checks to a shared failure: supplied evidence was
not incorporated into its required artifact. Agents should track
conditional obligations through the chosen response path, verifying that
the supporting explanation reaches its destination alongside the
numerical amendments.

### H.3. Procedural Transfer Across Cases

The third example follows an accepted Filer update into a later
first-pass task under the 16-task batch schedule. It comes from an
earlier 64-task run and supplies no additional observation to the main
380-task comparison. In the first completed batch, feedback identifies a
filing whose market-maker status remains inconsistent across the
Summary, other filing text, and Exhibit 99.2 (reference concern
r01:c05). The subsequent accepted guidance instructs Filer to project
its edits against the current draft, search the entire projected filing
for affected entities, numbers, statuses, and earlier wording, and
remove surviving contradictions. The skill is frozen for the next batch;
it transfers a verification procedure rather than the earlier issuer’s
market-maker facts.

In the later case (reference concern r01:c06), a risk factor states that
the company irrevocably opted out of the JOBS Act extended accounting
transition period, while several other passages disclose an election to
use it. Reviewer R1 cites the conflicting locations. Filer replaces the
opt-out statement with the supported election, adds the resulting
financial-statement comparability risk, and makes conforming changes in
the accounting note. The committed risk-factor text satisfies both
selected requirements: it reconciles the election and explains that the
financial statements may not be comparable to those of issuers adopting
standards on public-company effective dates. Requests for additional
company confirmation and adoption details remain separately identified.

Outcome and interpretation.
Figure [12](#A8.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ H.3. Procedural Transfer Across Cases ‣ Appendix H Case Studies and Failure Analysis ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision")
links the earlier inconsistency feedback, the accepted rule, and the
later document revisions. The subject changes from market-maker
arrangements to accounting elections, while the transferable operation
remains the same: locate competing statements, reconcile the supported
position across required locations, and inspect the resulting text.
Learning at this level supports a reusable action sequence without
turning a previous company’s answer into evidence for the current
issuer. It also makes the learned procedure inspectable: the rule
specifies what to search, which state to check, and what counts as
completion in the final artifact.

## Appendix I Limitations and Responsible Data Use

FilingLoop evaluates evidence-backed disclosure resolution in
reconstructed review interactions. Its conclusions concern the supplied
historical records, task eligibility rules, agents, and online protocol.
The following boundaries guide interpretation of the results and reuse
of the data and framework.

### I.1. Historical Reconstruction and Coverage

The corpus is concentrated on IPO registration review, with a
deliberately small annual-report extension from one existing issuer. It
spans domestic and foreign companies but does not represent every filing
type, jurisdiction, industry, or stage of regulatory review. The two
annual-report tasks extend the task format without establishing broad
annual-report generalization. Results should therefore be interpreted in
relation to the corpus composition in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Data Sources and Benchmark Construction ‣ FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision").

Historical correspondence records the concerns staff raised and the
responses that became available. It does not enumerate every defensible
concern or every acceptable resolution. FilingLoop consequently assesses
additional generated concerns on their evidence and substance rather
than treating an absent historical match as an error. Eligibility also
selects requirements whose requested actions and necessary facts have
attributable support. This makes fulfillment evaluable while limiting
conclusions about cases requiring unrecorded information, negotiations,
or other unavailable company evidence.

Temporal reconstruction controls what the agent can inspect, but cannot
establish what a language model encountered during pretraining. Public
filing and correspondence text may have appeared in training data.
Repeated rounds and requirements from the same company are also related
observations, so the number of requirements should not be read as the
number of independent companies or independent regulatory decisions
represented by the benchmark.

### I.2. Evaluator Validity and Online Adaptation

Model-assisted annotation and evaluation can misinterpret an accounting
question, overlook relevant context, or judge an alternative response
inconsistently. Independent annotation checks, source-linked
requirements, structured judgment schemas, and quotation validation
improve traceability, but mechanical validation does not establish
semantic correctness. The evaluator underwent manual review, and all
configurations share its grading model, prompts, and artifact checks.
Human–grader agreement and cross-grader sensitivity are not quantified.
Results are specific to the evaluated task sample and order in this
single seeded stream. The acting Reviewer and the independent evaluator
have different responsibilities; the former’s closure decision cannot
replace the latter’s requirement check.

The bounded fact service supplies historical evidence associated with
matched concerns. It does not reproduce unrestricted access to company
personnel or guarantee answers to arbitrarily phrased questions. Its
response reflects recorded evidence coverage, and a failed match is
distinct from an issuer’s inability to answer. The task therefore
measures fact acquisition within this defined interface rather than
every aspect of a live counsel–company exchange.

Evolution uses feedback from earlier tasks in the evaluation stream,
including earlier rounds of issuers that can reappear later. The
resulting comparison measures online procedural adaptation under the
specified order. It does not establish company-disjoint transfer or
robustness to every alternative stream order. Textual filters on learned
skills reject known identifiers and direct reference copying, but cannot
guarantee that all paraphrased case information has been excluded. Fixed
prompt precedence and case-specific evidence checks remain necessary
when applying learned procedures to subsequent disclosures.

Both roles receive procedural updates within the same interaction
protocol. The treatment in the paired comparison is therefore the joint
evolving policy, while role accuracies describe discovery and
conditional resolution within that treatment. Their denominators and
information dependencies should be preserved when interpreting
contributions at each stage. Framework comparisons likewise account for
native tool loops and measured expenditure alongside backbone identity
and the shared artifact contract.

### I.3. Source Attribution and Data Handling

The source records are public SEC filings and correspondence, and
derived tasks retain company, accession, date, and source-span
provenance. Role-private company answers are drawn from the same
historical collection. Their visibility is restricted to model the
Filer’s access to supporting evidence during an interaction, without
giving the Reviewer the hidden fact ledger. The term private therefore
describes a role boundary in the experiment and does not imply that
confidential issuer records or direct communications with company
personnel were obtained for evaluation. Released answers retain their
connection to the public source evidence used to construct each task.

Reuse should preserve document attribution and the distinction between
original statements, derived annotations, and model-generated revisions.
Names and other personal information can occur in public filings, so
distributing task examples requires attention to the specific fields and
source passages included. Credentials, account information, and
unrelated workspace files are excluded from task materials. Generated
figures use fictional characters and identify software roles rather than
depicting SEC officials or company representatives involved in the
source reviews.

### I.4. Intended Use and Human Oversight

The framework supports research on document-grounded review, revision,
and procedural learning. Generated comments and amendments are
experimental artifacts; they are not SEC communications, executed
agreements, obtained consents, or submitted filings. A successful edit
transaction proves that a specified document operation was committed,
not that the issuer performed an external action described in the text.

Practical use requires qualified review of the source evidence,
requested changes, accounting interpretation, and final deliverables.
Unsupported company assertions or inconsistent revisions can remain
consequential even when aggregate accuracy improves. The separate harm
audits and strict comment, task, and company metrics expose these
obligations rather than allowing a high requirement count to substitute
for complete verification of the documents and commitments on which a
real review decision depends.
````
